source_title: Kappler, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties vol. IV (1929), Unratified treaties, reprinting Senate Executive Journal
source_cite: Kappler IV 1081-1085, citing Senate Executive Journal vol. 8, pp. 417-419 (July 8, 1852)
source_quote: The eighteen treaties with Indian tribes in California received on the 7th and reported without amendment the 28th June, were severally read the second time
corrected_summary: Fillmore sent the 18 treaties to the Senate on June 1, 1852. The Senate received them June 7, the committee reported them without amendment June 28, and on July 8, 1852 the Senate unanimously refused consent to each treaty (Senate Executive Journal vol. 8, pp. 417-419). The injunction of secrecy was removed January 18, 1905 (NARA Prologue 2013, citing the Senate Executive Journal entry). Interior and the Indian Office recorded strong opposition among white Californians and in the California legislature and congressional delegation. The 'commissioner irregularities' reason is NARA's characterization. Acreage not checked here.
corrected_instrument_cite: Senate Executive Journal vol. 8, pp. 417-419 (July 8, 1852); Kappler IV 1081
notes: June 28, 1852 is the committee report date, not the vote, which explains the conflicting source. NARA Prologue's own sidebar quotes a 1904 Senate clerk letter giving July 2, 1852; the Journal extract printed in Kappler IV gives July 8. 1905 date: NARA Prologue 2013 (saved web/nara-prologue-2013-treaties.pdf) says Bard 'had the injunction of secrecy removed from the Senate's copies of the treaties on January 18'; the 1905 Senate Executive Journal itself was not reached (loc.gov llej pages return 403). Quote of Lea, May 14, 1852 (Kappler IV 1086): 'It was known that the delegation in Congress from California were opposed to the treaties, and that there was violent opposition to them in the legislature of that State'.

source_title: Indian Claims Commission, Thompson et al. (Indians of California) v. United States, Dockets 31, 37, 80, 80-D, 347 consolidated: Findings of Fact (Part 1) and Final Determination
source_cite: ICC Dockets 31, 37, 80, 80-D, 347 (consolidated), 13 Ind. Cl. Comm. 369, 543 (July 20, 1964); title phase 8 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1 (1959)
source_quote: do have and recover of and from the defendant the net sum of $29,100,000
corrected_summary: The ICC entered a single compromise judgment of $29,100,000 (net) on July 20, 1964 in consolidated Dockets 31, 37, 80, 80-D and 347 (Indians of California, Mission Bands, Pit River). The ICC held Indian title in California was extinguished by the Act of March 3, 1851 (9 Stat. 631) and the Act of March 3, 1853 (10 Stat. 244), with taking and valuation as of March 3, 1853. The ICC put net acreage at about 64,425,000 acres, which gives roughly 45 cents an acre. Pit River objectors are recorded in the settlement findings. The 1964 appropriation and the 1972 refusal of checks were not checked.
notes: Docket numbers now confirmed. Offsets row note: the ICC (8 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, 31) says the 1944 Court of Claims gross judgment was $17,058,941.98, reduced by offsets to a net of about $5,000,000. 'Taken ... March 3, 1853' matches ICC wording ('taken by the United States without compensation as of March 3, 1853, by the act of March 3, 1853'); the BIA press-release wording itself was not re-read. Settlement also barred offsets from March 3, 1853 to June 30, 1962.

source_title: Indian Claims Commission, Thompson et al. v. United States, Opinion of the Commission (title), Dockets 31 and 37
source_cite: 8 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, 31 (July 31, 1959), describing Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583 and 102 Ct. Cl. 837 (1944)
source_quote: the award was made on the basis of the value of the lands included in the 18 unratified treaties
corrected_summary: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 (45 Stat. 602), the Court of Claims gave the Indians of California a gross judgment of $17,058,941.98, reduced by offsets to a net recovery of about $5,000,000 (98 Ct. Cl. 583; 102 Ct. Cl. 837). The ICC later read that award as based on the value of the reserve lands promised in the 18 unratified treaties, not as payment for aboriginal title, and held that the Indians received no compensation for their aboriginal rights. The row's claim that the Court of Claims itself 'expressly said' it was not paying for a cession or taking is the ICC's later reading, not a quote from 102 Ct. Cl. 837.
corrected_instrument_cite: Act of May 18, 1928, 45 Stat. 602; Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583 (1942), 102 Ct. Cl. 837 (1944)
notes: The 1944 opinion itself was not reached (Court of Claims reports are not on govinfo or CAP static for 102 Ct. Cl.). ICC also notes 611,226 acres of reservation lands were charged as offsets at $1.25 an acre ($764,032.50). OCR prints the reporter as '132 C. Cls. 837' in one place; it is 102.

source_title: CERD, Early Warning and Urgent Action Procedure, Decision 1 (68), United States of America (Western Shoshone)
source_cite: CERD/C/USA/DEC/1 (11 April 2006), paras. 3-4, 6, 10; Pub. L. 108-270, 118 Stat. 805 (July 7, 2004)
source_quote: The Committee has received credible information alleging that the Western Shoshone indigenous peoples are being denied their traditional rights to land
corrected_summary: At its 68th session (20 Feb to 10 Mar 2006) CERD acted on requests from the Western Shoshone National Council, Timbisha Shoshone, Winnemucca Indian Colony and Yomba Shoshone. It found credible information that Western Shoshone are being denied traditional land rights and that US measures may cumulatively cause irreparable harm. The US did reply (letter of 15 Feb 2006) but did not answer the list of issues or appear; CERD regretted that. CERD cited the IACHR Dann decision (Case 11.140, 27 Dec 2002) that the ICC process did not meet international norms, and urged a freeze on privatization and on grazing fees, trespass notices and impoundments. The Western Shoshone Claims Distribution Act (Pub. L. 108-270, July 7, 2004) provides for distribution of Docket 326-K funds; the $145-160M figure was not checked.
notes: Correction: 'US had not responded' overstates; the US sent a letter but gave no substantive answers. IACHR report number 75/02 not read here; CERD cites the case by number and date only.

source_title: Cayuga Indian Nation of New York v. Pataki, 413 F.3d 266 (2d Cir. June 28, 2005)
source_quote: resulting in a total award of $247,911,999.42
notes: Opinion confirms: 64,015 acres; 1795 and 1807 New York 'treaties' never federally ratified; 1807 purchase of the remaining three-square-mile parcel for $4,800; district court award $247,911,999.42 (about $36.9M damages plus about $211M prejudgment interest); 'we reverse the judgment of the District Court and enter judgment for defendants' on laches under Sherrill. Row says 64,012 acres in 1795 plus 3 in 1807; the opinion gives 64,015 acres total and describes the 1807 parcel as three square miles, not three acres. Cert. denial not separately checked.

source_title: Mashpee Tribe v. New Seabury Corp., 592 F.2d 575 (1st Cir. Feb. 13, 1979); Final Determination for Federal Acknowledgment of the Mashpee Wampanoag Indian Tribal Council, 72 Fed. Reg. 8007 (Feb. 22, 2007)
source_quote: constitute an Indian tribe as of August 26, 1976: The date of the commencement of this law suit? No
corrected_summary: In a 40-day trial on tribal status (Oct. 1977 to Jan. 1978) the jury answered that the Mashpee were not a tribe on July 22, 1790, were a tribe on March 31, 1834 and March 3, 1842, and were not a tribe on June 23, 1869, May 28, 1870 or August 26, 1976. The First Circuit affirmed judgment for defendants. Interior's final determination acknowledging the Mashpee Wampanoag was published Feb. 22, 2007, effective May 23, 2007.
notes: Correction: the jury found the Mashpee WERE a tribe in 1834 and 1842; the 'not a tribe' answers were for 1790, 1869, 1870 and 1976. 'First Nonintercourse Act case tried to a jury' is not stated in the opinion; drop or source it.

source_title: NARA microfilm T494, Unratified Treaty File (UW Digital Collections list of titles)
source_cite: NARA T494, 'Documents relating to the negotiation of an unratified treaty of April 19, 1851, with the Kalapuya and Molala Indians'
source_quote: Documents relating to the negotiation of an unratified treaty of April 19, 1851, with the Kalapuya and Molala Indians
corrected_summary: The Willamette Valley Treaty Commission's 1851 treaties were never ratified; the T494 Unratified Treaty File holds at least one of them (April 19, 1851, Kalapuya and Molala). The other Champoeg treaties (Santiam, Tualatin, Yamhill, Luckiamute, Molala), Dart's advice and the 'effectively rejected through neglect' wording are from secondary sources (Oregon Encyclopedia; Lewis). The 1855 Kalapuya treaty (10 Stat. 1143) later ceded the valley.
corrected_instrument_cite: Unratified (NARA T494); successor: Treaty with the Kalapuya, etc., Jan. 22, 1855, 10 Stat. 1143
notes: Settling the full set and Dart's role needs ARCIA 1851 (Dart's report), which is not on archive.org under the usual usindianaffairs identifiers, and the UW 'History' collection pages were blocked earlier. 'Effectively rejected through neglect' is the Oregon Encyclopedia's phrase; attribute it.

source_title: Royce 1899 Schedule, area 687; Treaty with Mexico (Gadsden), Dec. 30, 1853; ICC Final Report (1978) docket table
source_cite: Royce 1899 area 687; 10 Stat. 1031; ICC Docket 345, 19 Ind. Cl. Comm. 394 (1968) (title); Dockets 102 and 345, 38 Ind. Cl. Comm. 542, 559 (July 21, 1976)
source_quote: No treaty of purchase was ever made with these tribes, who have a common
corrected_summary: The US acquired the area from Mexico by the Gadsden treaty (10 Stat. 1031), with no O'odham party. Royce 687 says no treaty of purchase was ever made with these tribes and the US took possession. The ICC found Papago title in Docket 345 (19 Ind. Cl. Comm. 394, Sept. 10, 1968) and entered a $26,000,000 compromise award in Dockets 102 and 345 on July 21, 1976.
corrected_royce_areas: 687 (Pima, Papago and related tribes of common origin)
notes: Docket 345 confirmed. Royce 687 is a joint entry for tribes 'who have a common origin' (Pima and Papago group), not Papago alone. Mapping note: the Gadsden line is an international boundary; much O'odham land lies in Sonora.

source_title: Indian Claims Commission Final Report (1978), Fiscal Year Totals of Dockets Completed and Awards; Esri FeatureServer metadata
source_cite: ICC Final Report (1978) p. 125 table; Esri FeatureServer layer 5
corrected_summary: The ICC Final Report's table shows 204 dockets completed by dismissal and 342 by award (546 total) through Sept. 30, 1978, with cumulative awards of $818,172,606.64. A public Esri FeatureServer exists with layer 5 'Indian Land Areas Judicially Established 1978', described as areas where a tribe proved original occupancy before the ICC or Court of Claims.
notes: Both 546 and $818.2M confirmed. The $1.3B figure likely adds Court of Claims judgments on transferred dockets after 1978; not checked. Esri layer licensing and the CATNUM-to-docket crosswalk were not checked. Note the 617 dockets filed versus 546 completed by the Commission itself.

source_title: Treaty with the Shawnee, Jan. 31, 1786 (Fort Finney)
source_cite: 7 Stat. 26, Arts. I-II
source_quote: Three hostages shall be immediately delivered to the Commissioners
corrected_summary: The treaty text confirms terms dictated to the Shawnee: Article I required three hostages to be delivered at once until captives were returned, and Article II made the Shawnee acknowledge US sovereignty. Partial attendance, reluctant signing by Moluntha's people and later renunciation remain secondary.
notes: Primary text adds a duress element (hostages, Art. I) the row lacks. Butler's 1785-86 journal (Craig, The Olden Time vol. 2) was downloaded (library/books3/oldentime-v2-oldentimemonthly02crai.txt) but the Fort Finney journal was not found in that OCR. Do not map 'about a third attended' until sourced (Calloway, The Shawnees and the War for America, 2007, not online).

source_title: George A. Custer, My Life on the Plains (1874), Project Gutenberg 73498
source_cite: Custer, My Life on the Plains (1874), ch. on Sweetwater (March 1869) and Fort Hays
source_quote: if by sunset the following day the two white girls were not restored to our hands unharmed, the lives of the three chiefs would be forfeited
corrected_summary: On the Sweetwater in March 1869 Custer seized four Cheyenne men as hostages, released one as a messenger, and told the rest their lives would be forfeited unless the two white captives were returned by sunset the next day. The three chiefs (Custer names Big Head, Dull Knife and Fat Bear) were taken to Fort Hays. There, during a transfer to the guard-house, a fight broke out with the guard: Big Head was killed, Dull Knife died of a bayonet wound, and Fat Bear survived and was later released.
notes: Correction: Custer threatens that their lives would be forfeited; he does not say hanging in this passage (hanging is in other accounts). Custer gives the deaths as a fight with the guard, not 'attempting to escape'. Custer is a self-interested source; George Bent's names differ.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (quoting secondary history)
source_cite: Harney's report, Sept. 5, 1855, in Annual Report of the Secretary of War 1855 (S. Ex. Doc. 1, 34th Cong., 1st sess., pt. 2)
notes: The document that settles 86 killed and about 70 captives is Harney's own report in the 1855 Secretary of War annual report. It is not in the library, archive.org search returned no 1855 War report, and HathiTrust and loc.gov serial set pages return 403. The library's SecWar volumes are 1857, 1868-69 and 1876-77. R. Eli Paul, Blue Water Creek and the First Sioux War (2004), is in copyright. Keep the numbers attributed to Harney's report as quoted by the PSL book.

source_title: MNHS, 'The Traders' Paper' (U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 site)
source_cite: MNHS Traders' Paper page; 10 Stat. 949
source_quote: turned over about a third of the Dakotas' cash payments to a group of traders, including Henry Sibley and his associates
corrected_summary: After signing the Traverse des Sioux treaty in 1851, Sisseton and Wahpeton leaders signed a separate Traders' Paper that some later said they were tricked into signing; it assigned about a third of their cash payments to traders including Henry Sibley's associates. The claim that the 1852 annuity was withheld until the Dakota accepted the settlement is not on the MNHS page and was not checked in a primary source.
notes: The settling document is the Senate investigation of Gov. Ramsey (S. Ex. Doc. 61, 33d Cong., 1st sess., 1854) with testimony; it is in the Serial Set (HathiTrust/loc.gov 403 here). The NPS Traverse des Sioux NRHP nomination quoted by the row was not reached.

source_title: Treaty of Medicine Creek, Dec. 26, 1854; Treaty of Point Elliott, Jan. 22, 1855
corrected_summary: Treaty texts confirm the instruments but say nothing about the language of interpretation. The Chinook Jargon interpretation is the standard account of the councils; the 300 to 400 word figure is a critic's estimate reported by Crosscut, not a primary fact.
notes: Settle with the official proceedings of the Point Elliott and Medicine Creek councils (Records of the Washington Superintendency, NARA M5, roll 26), not online here. On the map, attribute the 'trade jargon' note to named critics.

source_title: Treaty with the Osage, Nov. 10, 1808 (Fort Clark)
source_cite: 7 Stat. 107; Kappler II 95
corrected_summary: Treaty text confirms the Nov. 10, 1808 cession at Fort Clark. The claims that Osage leaders rejected Clark's September version because they were absent and that White Hair was a 'government chief' without authority rest on secondary sources.
notes: Settle with Clark and Lewis correspondence in Territorial Papers of the United States vol. 14 (Louisiana-Missouri), not online here, or Louis Burns, A History of the Osage People (in copyright).

source_title: Report of the Ute Commission, in Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1881
source_cite: ARCIA 1881, Report of Ute Commission pp. 203-204; 21 Stat. 199
source_quote: the names obtained at both agencies aggregated 581 adult male Ute Indians of the confederated bands in Colorado
corrected_summary: The Ute Commission's own report confirms the Southern Utes at first refused to ratify, Ouray died on Aug. 24, 1880 during the councils, and the commission then gathered marks band by band until it counted 581 adult males, which it judged above three-fourths. Mears was a member and disbursing officer. The report says nothing about $2-per-signature payments; that claim rests on Conetah as quoted by the PSL book.
notes: Correction: the official count was 581, not about 527. The report also notes Weeminuche who 'would move in and do so when the money promised them arrived'. Keep BRIBERY only attributed to Conetah (A History of the Northern Ute People, 1982, not read).

source_title: Act of March 3, 1893, ch. 203, ratifying the Kickapoo agreement of June 21, 1891
source_quote: when I explained it to said Whipple he pretended to interpret it to said Indians, in full council assembled
corrected_summary: The ratified text confirms the Kickapoo insisted on going to Washington to put their demand for a diminished reservation held in common to the Secretary of the Interior. The interpreter, Joseph Whipple, signed his certificate by mark; his certificate says he speaks and understands English and Kickapoo. Attorney John T. Hill certified that Whipple 'pretended to interpret' the power of attorney. The text does not say the interpreter certified that he could not read or write.
notes: Downloaded full chapter (govinfo STATUTE-27-Pg557-2, 7 pp.) to library/stat/STAT-27-557-2.pdf/.txt. Hill was also paid $5,172 from the proceeds (p. 563). Allotment schedules approved 1894 not checked.

source_title: Minot State University digital history (advocacy)
source_cite: S. Rep. No. 1522 / S. Ex. Doc. 70, 48th Cong., 1st sess. (Dawes committee on the Sioux agreement)
notes: The settling document is the Dawes select committee report and testimony on the Edmunds commission (48th Cong., 1st sess., 1883-84) in the Serial Set; HathiTrust and loc.gov return 403 here and it is not in the library (ARCIA 1883 has no Edmunds or Hinman passage in the OCR). Non-ratification itself is not in doubt.

source_title: Treaty with the Chippewa, Sept. 24, 1819 (Saginaw)
source_cite: 7 Stat. 203; Kappler II 185
corrected_summary: Treaty text confirms reserves to named individuals. That they were trader Jacob Smith's children, that Cass supplied five barrels of whiskey, and that Cass led the Saginaw to believe they kept their lands come from a modern court filing (U.S. v. Michigan) and later claims, not from the treaty.
notes: Settle with Cass's 1819 report to the War Department (Territorial Papers vol. 10, Michigan) or the exhibits to the U.S. v. Michigan filing. Attribute the whiskey claim to that filing.

source_title: Royce 1899 Schedule, Sept. 26, 1833, Chicago; Treaty of Chicago
source_cite: Royce 1899, Chicago Sept. 26, 1833 entry; 7 Stat. 431; Kappler II 402
source_quote: supposed to contain about 5,000,000 acres
corrected_summary: Royce confirms the united Chippewa, Ottawa and Potawatomi ceded their land along the western shore of Lake Michigan (about 5,000,000 acres) for a tract of not less than 5,000,000 acres west of the Mississippi. The schedules in the treaty pay large sums for claims. The 1902 Wisconsin Potawatomi petition and the liquor and trader-capture details were not checked.
notes: Royce describes the cession as 'along the western shore of Lake Michigan', mostly present Wisconsin and northeast Illinois. Keep BRIBERY_FRAUD_FORGERY only with a named scholar (e.g. Latrobe's eyewitness account, not read).

source_title: Treaty with the Winnebago and United Tribes of Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa, Aug. 25, 1828 (Green Bay)
source_cite: 7 Stat. 315, preamble; Kappler II 292
source_quote: the occupation, by white persons, of that part of the mining country which has not been heretofore ceded to the United States
corrected_summary: The 1828 Green Bay agreement records that the Winnebago and the United Tribes declined to cede, and that a provisional boundary was set to deal with white occupation of unceded mining country. The 1829 Prairie du Chien treaty (7 Stat. 323) then ceded the lead region. Red Bird's imprisonment and the 1827 war are not in these texts.
corrected_instrument_cite: 7 Stat. 323; Kappler II 300 (and 7 Stat. 315 for the 1828 provisional agreement)
notes: Primary support for 'intruder occupation preceded cession'. The Kappler II page of the 1828 agreement in this OCR is around p. 292 (S. Doc. 452); verify page before citing.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Sept. 17, 1851, full text with signatures
source_cite: 11 Stat. 749 (text as printed in Kappler IV 1065-1067), Art. 6
source_quote: having selected principals or head chiefs for their respective nations, through whom all national business will hereafter be conducted
corrected_summary: Article 6 records that each nation had 'selected' a head chief through whom all national business would be conducted, and binds the nations to sustain those chiefs. The first Sioux signer is Mah-toe-wha-you-whey (Conquering Bear). That the commissioners picked him and Big Robber when the nations would not, and that most Lakota did not recognize his authority, rests on secondary sources.
corrected_instrument_cite: Kappler IV 1065 (full text with signatures); Kappler II 594
notes: Treaty language says the Indians 'selected' the chiefs; the 'arbitrarily picked' claim contradicts the text and needs Mitchell's 1851 report (ARCIA 1851, not online here) or council press accounts. Identification of Mah-toe-wha-you-whey as Conquering Bear is standard but not stated in the treaty.

source_title: Royce 1899, introduction (C. Thomas), New York, quoting the Fort Stanwix deed of 1768
source_cite: Royce 1899 p. 584, quoting the deed of Nov. 5, 1768 (N.Y. Colonial Documents vol. 8)
source_quote: beginning at the Mouth of Cherokee or Hogohege River where it emptys into the River Ohio and running from thence upwards along the South side of said River to Kittaning
corrected_summary: The 1768 Fort Stanwix deed, quoted in Royce's introduction, records the Six Nations granting to the Crown the land south and east of a line beginning at the mouth of the Cherokee (Tennessee) River and running up the Ohio to Kittanning. That the Shawnee, Delaware and Cherokee who used Kentucky had no role, the 27-million-acre figure and the link to Dunmore's War are secondary (Campbell, Speculators in Empire).
corrected_instrument_cite: Colonial (Crown) deed, Nov. 5, 1768; quoted in Royce 1899 p. 584
notes: Correction to instrument_cite: the deed IS quoted in Royce 1899 (introduction p. 584), though not in the Schedule or Kappler.

source_cite: Henderson and Company purchase depositions (Virginia and North Carolina investigations, 1777-78)
corrected_instrument_cite: Private purchase (Transylvania Co.), Mar. 17, 1775; not in Kappler or Royce
notes: Royce 1899 has no Henderson or Transylvania entry (searched). The settling documents are the 1777 Virginia depositions on the Henderson purchase (printed in Virginia State Papers vol. 1 and Calendar of Virginia State Papers), not in the library; archive.org copies were not located in this pass. Dragging Canoe's 'dark and bloody' warning is tradition from later depositions; attribute it.

source_title: Treaty with the Delawares, etc., Sept. 30, 1809 (Fort Wayne)
source_cite: 7 Stat. 113; Kappler II 101
corrected_summary: Treaty text confirms the Delaware, Potawatomi, Miami and Eel River parties. Tecumseh's argument that land was held in common by all nations is from his August 1810 Vincennes speech as recorded by Harrison's side; it was not read here.
notes: Settle with Esarey, ed., Messages and Letters of William Henry Harrison vol. 1 (1922), which prints the Vincennes council; not in the library.

source_title: Treaty with the Osage, Sept. 25, 1818; Treaty with the Osage, June 2, 1825
source_cite: 7 Stat. 183, Art. 1; 7 Stat. 240
source_quote: both before and since their war with the Cherokees
corrected_summary: The 1818 text says the Osage ceded the Lovely's Purchase tract because claims for property taken by their war parties (before and since their war with the Cherokees) would otherwise consume their annuities for years. That confirms the Cherokee-Osage war and a cession driven by claims against annuities. That the US encouraged the war and then assigned the land to removed nations is interpretive and needs a named scholar.
notes: Burns, A History of the Osage People, not read. Royce entry numbers 97 and 123 not re-checked.

source_title: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1873 (Commissioner's report; Report of Capt. M. C. Wilkinson, Dec. 12, 1873); ARCIA 1878
source_cite: ARCIA 1873 pp. 14, and Wilkinson report; ARCIA 1878 Modoc paragraph
source_quote: Captain Jack and three of his principal men were tried by court-martial and executed
corrected_summary: The Commissioner's 1873 report confirms Captain Jack and three others were tried by court-martial and executed and the rest of the band was moved to the Indian Territory. Capt. Wilkinson took them by rail from Fort McPherson, Nebraska (Nov. 14, 1873) to Baxter Springs and settled them at Seneca Station on Shawnee land under the Quapaw agent. ARCIA 1878 counts 112 survivors. The Oct. 3, 1873 date and the figure of about 153 were not confirmed here.
corrected_instrument_cite: 16 Stat. 707 (1864 treaty); removal by War Department order, no instrument
notes: No treaty or agreement for the 1873 removal appears in these reports.

source_title: Act of March 2, 1889 (Sioux agreement)
source_cite: 25 Stat. 888
corrected_summary: The 1889 Act is confirmed. Ration cuts before and after signing, feasts, and pressure by the Crook Commission are secondary here.
notes: Settle with the Crook Commission report (S. Ex. Doc. 51, 51st Cong., 1st sess., 1890) and ARCIA 1889-1890, not in the library (archive.org usindianaffairs89/90 not present under that identifier). Ostler (Plains Sioux and U.S. Colonialism) not read.

source_title: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1884, Blackfeet Agency report (Agent Allen per the report index), Aug. 14, 1884
source_cite: ARCIA 1884 pp. 106-107 (Blackfeet Agency report, Aug. 14, 1884); 25 Stat. 113
source_quote: many of them were gradually dying of starvation
corrected_summary: The Blackfeet agent's 1884 report confirms that when he took charge on April 1, 1884 the Indians (about 2,300) were in deplorable condition, many dying of starvation, children emaciated and many since dead, with rations of a few ounces a day and people eating inner bark. The 1888 Act (25 Stat. 113) ratifies the 1886-87 agreement. The 'several hundred' and 'quarter or more' death figures and the 17.5 million acres were not confirmed.
notes: The report index lists it as 'Blackfeet Agency, Montana, annual report of Agent Allen'; the agent took charge April 1, 1884. Ewers, The Blackfeet, not read.

source_title: Treaty with the Cherokee, July 8, 1817
source_cite: 7 Stat. 156; Kappler II 140
corrected_summary: Treaty text confirms the exchange of eastern land for land on the Arkansas and the role of the Arkansas Cherokee and their deputies (John D. Chisholm and others). The National Council protest and the women's petitions are not in the treaty and were not checked.
notes: Settle with the Cherokee women's petitions of 1817-18 (printed in Perdue and Green) or McLoughlin, Cherokee Renascence; not in the library.

source_title: Report of the Indian Peace Commission, Jan. 7, 1868
source_cite: Indian Peace Commission report (1868), pp. 4-5, 9
source_quote: he at once ordered the Indian village, of about three hundred lodges together with the entire property of the tribes, to be burned
corrected_summary: The Peace Commission's own report confirms Hancock had the Cheyenne-Lakota village of about 300 lodges on Pawnee Fork burned, that the Cheyenne at Medicine Lodge stayed about forty miles off for two weeks out of suspicion, and that the joint Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty was made only after they arrived. The military escort and the gap between oral promises about hunting south of the Arkansas and the written terms were not confirmed here.
notes: Oral-vs-written gap: settle with the council proceedings (reporters' transcripts; Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge, 1966). Art. 11 of 15 Stat. 593 does reserve hunting south of the Arkansas 'so long as the buffalo may range', which partly supports the oral assurances.

source_title: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1864; Kappler I, Executive orders, Mescalero (Fort Stanton) reserve
source_cite: CIA 1864 (Steck/Superintendent report on Mescaleros); Kappler I, Mescalero Apache Reservation, Executive order May 29, 1873
source_quote: About four hundred of the Mescaleros are now, under the direction of their active and efficient agent, Mr. Labadi, living upon the reservation
corrected_summary: About 400 Mescalero were held at Bosque Redondo in 1864 under agent Labadi. Their later reservation came by executive order (May 29, 1873, replaced 1874 onward). No ratified treaty ceded Mescalero land, but Meriwether did make an unratified 1855 treaty with the Mescaleros and Mimbres. The Nov. 1865 flight was not checked here.
corrected_instrument_cite: No instrument for confinement; Executive Order May 29, 1873 (Kappler I)
notes: Change category from HOSTAGE to REMOVAL/CONFINEMENT. NEVER_CEDED is accurate only for ratified instruments; note the unratified 1855 Meriwether treaty (see WEB-UR-013). A peace treaty with the Apache of July 1, 1852 (10 Stat. 979) exists but has no cession.

source_title: John Mason, A Brief History of the Pequot War (Boston, 1736), archive.org briefhistoryofpe00maso
source_cite: Mason 1736, pp. 30-31 and 38-39 (as reprinted)
source_quote: themselves utterly Destroyed, to the Number of six or seven Hundred, as some of themselves confessed. There were only seven taken captive, and about seven escaped
corrected_instrument_cite: Colonial; Hartford covenant of 1638 (not in Kappler or Royce)
notes: Mason, the English commander, gives six or seven hundred killed (Underhill's tract, quoted in the same volume, 'about 700' slain and taken). Mason also records the Hartford terms: survivors divided (80 to Uncas, 80 to Miantonomo, 20 to Ninigret) and 'none should inhabit their native Country, nor should any of them be called Pequots any more'.
